nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life on land|Habitat restoration|Mountain habitat restoration_qna_000
nodes.label: Ecology
nodes.question: What broader pressures are Alpine habitats facing that affect their seasonality and habitat structure?
nodes.answer: Alpine habitats are under pressure from climate change and land-use modifications, which lead to changes in seasonality, habitat structure, and eventually to population declines.
nodes.paragraph: Introduction Organisms in seasonal habitats face multiple challenges when breeding within a restricted period with favourable conditions (Lack 1968; Martin and Wiebe 2004; Perrins 1970). In temperate mountain habitats, the availability of suitable habitat and the abundance of food resources change over the breeding season and may vary between years (Mar - tin 2001). In a broader time frame, Alpine habitats are under pressure from climate change and land-use modifications, leading to changes in seasonality and habitat structure and eventually to population declines (La Sorte and Jetz 2010; Chamberlain et al. 2013; Lehikoinen et al. 2014; Scridel et al. 2018). Breeding ecology is central to understand the underlying mechanisms of population trends. The selection of a suitable nesting site affects breeding success and is usually driven by environmental factors (Hinde 1956; Martin 1993). The fac- tors related to the selection of a nest site are often similar to, but not necessarily the same as, those influencing breeding success per se (Arlt and P rt 2007; Gilroy et al. 2011).

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life on land|Habitat restoration|Mountain habitat restoration_qna_001
nodes.label: Ecology
nodes.question: How do topographic characteristics affect bird breeding success?
nodes.answer: Topographic characteristics such as elevation, slope, and aspect can influence the microhabitat and microclimate of a nest, which in turn can affect incubation behavior and breeding success in high-Alpine bird species.
nodes.paragraph: The selection of breeding habitats often depends on the avail - ability of suitable nest locations, but also on the suitability of the surrounding habitat, especially for foraging and feeding the nestlings (Brambilla et al. 2017; Resano-Mayor et al. 2019; Barras et al. 2020). While access to food resources is key to breeding success, other factors such as predation risk may influence the choice of a breeding site (Martin 1993 ; Low et al. 2010; Schneider et al. 2012). Moreover, for bird species that rely on the same territory during their presence in the breeding region, the suitability of the habitat is also important during the pre- and post-breeding periods (Arlt and P rt 2008; M ller et al. 2023). Topographic characteristics such as elevation, slope, and aspect often influence the microhabitat and the microcli- mate of a nest and hence can influence incubation behaviour and breeding success in high-Alpine bird species (Camfield and Martin 2009 ; MacDonald et al. 2016 ; Niffenegger et al. 2023a, b). Habitat structures in the surroundings of the nest, including perches and shelter for the fledglings, can also explain nest site selection.

nodes.question: What drives the abundance and accessibility of food resources in Alpine environments?
nodes.answer: Vegetation development, which generally follows snowmelt, drives the abundance and accessibility of food resources in Alpine environments.
nodes.paragraph: Vegetation development, which generally follows snowmelt in Alpine environments, drives the abundance of food resources and also their accessibility (Brambilla et al. 2017; Resano-Mayor et al. 2019; Barras et al. 2020; M ller et al. 2023). For ground-foraging birds, shrub and fast-growing grass reduce access to food. On the other hand, short swards and bare ground improve accessi- bility (Schaub et al. 2010; Tagmann-loset et al. 2012; M ller et al. 2023). Social factors, such as intra-specific competi- tion, as well as predation, often influence nest site selection and breeding success (Lack 1968; Martin 1993). nodes.question: What type of habitats were the high-altitude populations sampled from?
nodes.answer: The high-altitude populations were sampled from unfertilized alpine meadows in the central Alps.
nodes.paragraph: ), and from four replicated high-altitude populations in Austria (L. tityrus subalpinus; K htai: 47.23 N, 10.97 E; Obernberg: 46.98 N, 11.42 E; Obergurgl: 46.86 N, 11.2 E; Venn: 47.1 N, 11.54 E; alti- tudinal range 1560 2030 m a.s.l.). All high-altitude popula - tions were sampled on unfertilized alpine meadows in the central Alps, i.e., above crystalline primary rock (gneiss, slate) resulting in acidic, nutrient-poor soils. The low-alti- tude populations, in contrast, originate from slightly ferti- lized meadows from areas that are also naturally richer in nutrients (basalt mountains or marshland). Note that sam- pling locations not only differed in altitude but also in lati- tude. However, the impact of variation in altitude is expected to surpass the potential impact of latitude by far (Karl et al. 2008 , 2009a ). Per population, we sampled between 6 and 20 females, in total 34 from low- and 48 from high-altitude populations. Females were afterwards transferred to and randomly distributed among two climate cabinets (26 C, 70% humidity, L19:D5 photoperiod; Panasonic MIR-554) at Koblenz University for egg laying.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life on land|Habitat restoration|Mountain habitat restoration_qna_004
nodes.label: Ecology and conservation
nodes.question: Between which elevational ranges were healthier M. aculeata populations found?
nodes.answer: Healthier M. aculeata populations were found in the middle elevational range of 3700 m to 4100 m.
nodes.paragraph: Globally, alpine environments are most significantly affected by climate change, characterized by low temperatures and restricted growing seasons, offering essential services yet remaining most vulnerable. M. aculeata holds immense ecological significance in alpine ecosystems, while human disturbances and climate change pose serious threats to its long-term viability. The present study was conducted to explore population ecology, spatial distribution patterns, significant threats, diversity patterns along elevational gradients, and future conservation strategies for the dwindling populations of M. aculeata . Methods Field sampling was carried out from 2022 to 2024 in various districts of Kashmir to examine the vegetation characteristics of M. aculeata populations, along with the geographic variables and threats impacting these populations. The quadrat method was used to investigate the vegetation characteristics across an extensive elevational gradient, ranging from 3000 m to 4600 m. Results Healthier M. aculeata populations were found in the middle elevational range of 3700 m to 4100 m. The SIMPER analysis revealed an overall average dissimilarity of 80.8, indicating spatial variability in species composition across the studied sites. GIS analysis showed that M. aculeata was found on the north aspect, with steppe slope in rocky habitat.
